dsp-001.question: A 6 kHz sine wave is sampled at a sampling frequency of 48 kHz. Which of the following is the normalized angular frequency ω (the phase advance per sample) of the resulting discrete-time signal?
dsp-001.explanation: The normalized angular frequency is ω = 2πf/fs and tells how far the phase advances during one sample. ω = 2π × 6 kHz ÷ 48 kHz = 2π × 0.125 = π/4 rad/sample. f/fs = 0.125 means "0.125 cycles per sample", so one period takes 8 samples. The Nyquist frequency of 24 kHz corresponds to ω = π, and discrete-time frequencies are considered in the range −π to π.
choiceNotes: This is f/fs, whose unit is cycles per sample. To express it in radians, multiply by 2π.
This multiplies by π instead of 2π (π × 6/48 = π/8).
Correct. 2π × 6/48 = π/4 rad/sample.

dsp-002.question: Which of the following is the fundamental period (the smallest positive integer N such that x[n + N] = x[n] for every integer n) of the discrete-time signal x[n] = cos(0.3πn)?
choices: It has no period (it is not periodic)
dsp-002.explanation: A discrete-time sinusoid cos(ω₀n) is periodic only when ω₀/2π is a rational number k/N (in lowest terms), and its fundamental period is then N. Here ω₀/2π = 0.3π/2π = 0.15 = 3/20, so N = 20 samples (exactly 3 cycles fit in them). Thinking in continuous time, 2π/ω₀ ≈ 6.67 is not an integer, so the sample positions shift from one cycle to the next. When ω₀/2π is irrational, as for cos(n) with ω₀/2π = 1/(2π), the same sequence of values never returns, so the signal is not periodic.
choiceNotes: 2π/ω₀ = 2/0.3 ≈ 6.67 is the continuous-time period. Sample indices are integers, so the values do not repeat every 6.67 samples.
Correct. 0.3π/2π = 3/20, so after 20 samples (3 cycles) the sequence returns to its start.
ω₀/2π = 0.15 is rational, so the signal is periodic. It is not periodic only when ω₀/2π is irrational.

dsp-003.question: Which of the following signals takes the same value as the discrete-time signal x[n] = cos(1.75πn) for every integer n?
dsp-003.explanation: Because n is an integer, a discrete-time sinusoid gives exactly the same sequence of values when its angular frequency is shifted by 2π. cos(1.75πn) = cos(1.75πn − 2πn) = cos(−0.25πn), and since cos is an even function this equals cos(0.25πn). This is aliasing seen from the digital side: a frequency above ω = π cannot be told apart from the lower frequency 2π − ω. In terms of the sampling frequency, a sine wave at 0.875fs gives the same samples as one at 0.125fs.
choiceNotes: Correct. 1.75π − 2π = −0.25π, and cos is even, so the values are the same.
This subtracts π from 1.75π. A shift of π gives cos(1.75πn) = (−1)ⁿcos(0.75πn), so the odd-numbered samples change sign.
This is 1.75π divided by 2. Halving the angular frequency does not give the same sequence of values.

dsp-004.question: Which of the following correctly relates the unit impulse δ[n] (1 at n = 0, 0 elsewhere) and the unit step u[n] (1 for n ≥ 0, 0 for n < 0)?
dsp-004.explanation: Subtracting u[n − 1], the step delayed by one sample, from u[n] gives 1 − 1 = 0 for n ≥ 1, 1 − 0 = 1 at n = 0 and 0 for n < 0, which is δ[n]. Conversely, u[n] is the running sum of δ[n] up to n. This expresses the continuous-time relation "the derivative of a step is an impulse, and the integral of an impulse is a step" with a difference and a running sum.
choiceNotes: The sum is 1 at n = 0 and 2 for n ≥ 1.
The product is 1 for n ≥ 1, which is the same as u[n − 1].
Correct. The difference from the step delayed by one sample remains only at n = 0.

dsp-005.question: Which of the following is the energy E = Σ|x[n]|² of x[n] = (0.5)ⁿu[n] (0.5 to the power n for n ≥ 0, 0 for n < 0)?
dsp-005.explanation: Energy is the sum of the squares of all samples. Since |x[n]|² = (0.25)ⁿ, the geometric series formula gives E = 1/(1 − 0.25) = 4/3 ≈ 1.33. The energy is finite, so this is an energy signal and its average power is 0.
choiceNotes: Correct. The square of (0.5)ⁿ is (0.25)ⁿ, and the sum is 1/(1 − 0.25) = 4/3.
This adds the amplitudes without squaring them (1/(1 − 0.5) = 2).
This squares the sum of the amplitudes, 2. The sum of squares and the square of the sum are different.

dsp-006.question: Which of the following is the average power (the mean of |x[n]|² over one period) of x[n] = 2cos(πn/4)?
dsp-006.explanation: The average power of a sine wave of amplitude A is A²/2, so for A = 2 it is 4/2 = 2. Averaging the squares of the 8 samples in one period (2, √2, 0, −√2, −2, −√2, 0, √2) also gives (4 + 2 + 0 + 2 + 4 + 2 + 0 + 2)/8 = 2. A periodic signal has infinite energy, so its size is expressed by its average power instead (a power signal).
choiceNotes: Correct. A²/2 = 4/2 = 2.
This is the peak value squared (A² = 4). The mean of a squared sine wave is half the peak value squared.
This is the sum of the squares of the 8 samples in one period. The average power is this divided by the 8 samples.

dsp-007.question: Which of the following systems with input x[n] and output y[n] is both linear and time-invariant (LTI)?
dsp-007.explanation: Linearity means that a weighted sum of inputs gives the same weighted sum of outputs, and time invariance means that delaying the input by k samples only delays the output by k samples. y[n] = 3x[n] − x[n − 2] only multiplies the present and past inputs by constants and adds them, so it satisfies both. y[n] = x[n] + 2 outputs 2 even for a zero input, so it is not linear, and y[n] = x[−n] reverses time, so delaying the input makes the output earlier and it is not time-invariant.
choiceNotes: Adding the constant 2 gives an output of 2 even for a zero input, so superposition fails and the system is not linear.
It is linear, but because it reverses time, delaying the input makes the output earlier, so it is not time-invariant.
Correct. It adds the present and past inputs with constant coefficients, so it is linear and time-invariant.

dsp-008.question: Which of the following correctly describes the system y[n] = n·x[n]?
choices: It is linear and also time-invariant
It is linear but not time-invariant
It is not linear but it is time-invariant
dsp-008.explanation: The output for the input a·x₁[n] + b·x₂[n] is n(a·x₁[n] + b·x₂[n]) = a·y₁[n] + b·y₂[n], so the system is linear. However, the output for the delayed input x[n − k] is n·x[n − k], while the delayed output is (n − k)·x[n − k], and the two differ. For example, the input δ[n − 1] gives δ[n − 1], but δ[n − 2] gives 2δ[n − 2], so the response is not simply the same shape delayed. A system whose multiplier changes with the time index n is linear but not time-invariant.
choiceNotes: It is linear, but the multiplier n changes with time, so it is not time-invariant.
Correct. Superposition holds, but delaying the input does not simply delay the same output shape.
A sum of inputs gives the sum of outputs (superposition holds), so it is linear. It is also not time-invariant.

dsp-009.question: Which of the following systems with input x[n] and output y[n] is causal (its output depends only on inputs up to the present time)?
dsp-009.explanation: In a causal system, the output at time n depends only on inputs at or before time n (and on past outputs). y[n] = x[n] + 0.5y[n − 1] uses only the present input and the previous output, so it is causal and can be computed in real time. The other two contain x[n + 1], a future input that has not arrived yet, so they are not causal. When recorded data is processed afterwards, for example, processing that uses values on both sides can still be realized by delaying the output.
choiceNotes: It uses the next input x[n + 1], so it is not causal.
Correct. It can be computed from the present input and a past output only.
This is the average of three values around n and contains the future input x[n + 1], so it is not causal.

dsp-010.question: Let u[n] be the unit step. Which of the following LTI systems, given by their impulse responses, is BIBO stable (every bounded input gives a bounded output)?
dsp-010.explanation: An LTI system is BIBO stable if and only if the sum of the absolute values of its impulse response, Σ|h[n]|, is finite. For h[n] = (−0.9)ⁿu[n], Σ|h[n]| = Σ0.9ⁿ = 1/(1 − 0.9) = 10, which is finite, so the system is stable. h[n] = u[n] is an accumulator that keeps adding its input; the sum is infinite, and a constant input makes the output grow without limit. (1.1)ⁿ grows with time, so that system is unstable.
choiceNotes: Correct. The sign alternates, but Σ|h[n]| = 10 is finite.
This is the impulse response of an accumulator; Σ|h[n]| is infinite, so it is not stable. A step input makes the output grow as n + 1.
Since |1.1| > 1, h[n] keeps growing and the system is unstable.

dsp-011.question: The sequence x[n] = {1, 2, 3} (n = 0, 1, 2) is applied to an LTI system with impulse response h[n] = {1, −1} (n = 0, 1). Which of the following are the outputs y[0] to y[3]?
dsp-011.explanation: For h[n] = {1, −1}, the convolution y[n] = Σx[k]h[n − k] becomes y[n] = x[n] − x[n − 1], the difference from the previous input. y[0] = 1 − 0 = 1, y[1] = 2 − 1 = 1, y[2] = 3 − 2 = 1 and y[3] = 0 − 3 = −3. The output length is 3 + 2 − 1 = 4, from the input length 3 and the impulse-response length 2.
choiceNotes: This is computed without time-reversing h (a cross-correlation); its signs are opposite to the correct output.
This is the convolution with {1, 1}, dropping the sign of h[1].
Correct. It computes the difference from the previous input, x[n] − x[n − 1].

dsp-012.question: A unit step (x[n] = 1 for n ≥ 0) is applied from n = 0 to the system described by the difference equation y[n] = x[n] + 0.5y[n − 1]. With y[−1] = 0, which of the following is y[2]?
dsp-012.explanation: Step by step, y[0] = 1 + 0.5 × 0 = 1, y[1] = 1 + 0.5 × 1 = 1.5 and y[2] = 1 + 0.5 × 1.5 = 1.75. Continuing gives y[n] = 2 − 0.5ⁿ, which approaches the final value 1/(1 − 0.5) = 2. Because past outputs are used (there is feedback), this is an IIR filter whose impulse response 0.5ⁿ continues forever.
choiceNotes: Correct. The output goes 1 → 1.5 → 1.75.
This is y[3]. y[2] is two steps after y[0].
This is the final value 1/(1 − 0.5) as n → ∞, which has not been reached at y[2].

dsp-013.question: A signal sampled at 48 kHz is analyzed with a 1024-point discrete Fourier transform (DFT). Which of the following is the spacing of the frequency bins?
dsp-013.explanation: The bin spacing of an N-point DFT is Δf = fs/N, and 48000 ÷ 1024 = 46.875 Hz ≈ 46.9 Hz. Bin k corresponds to the frequency k × Δf: k = 0 is DC and k = N/2 = 512 is the Nyquist frequency of 24 kHz. Δf is also the reciprocal of the observation time T = N/fs ≈ 21.3 ms, so finer bins require a longer observation time.
choiceNotes: This is fs/(2N) = 24000 ÷ 1024. The bin spacing is fs/N.
This divides fs by the number of positive-frequency bins, N/2 = 512 (48000 ÷ 512).

dsp-014.question: Let k = 0 be the DC bin. When a 1 kHz sine wave sampled at 8 kHz is analyzed with a 256-point DFT, which of the following is the index k of the bin where the peak appears on the positive-frequency side?
dsp-014.explanation: The bin spacing is Δf = fs/N = 8000 ÷ 256 = 31.25 Hz, so 1 kHz falls in bin k = 1000 ÷ 31.25 = 32. 1 kHz is an exact multiple of the bin spacing (exactly 32 cycles in 256 samples), so the peak is concentrated in the single bin k = 32 and there is no spectral leakage. For a real signal, a peak of the same size also appears at k = N − 32 = 224, which corresponds to the negative frequency.
choiceNotes: This divides by the Nyquist frequency of 4 kHz instead of 8 kHz (1000 × 256/4000).
k = N/2 = 128 is the bin of the Nyquist frequency (4 kHz).

dsp-015.question: A 64-point DFT of a real signal x[n] gives X[10] = 3 + 4j. Which of the following is X[54]?
dsp-015.explanation: The DFT of a real signal is conjugate symmetric: X[N − k] = X[k]* (the complex conjugate of X[k]). With N = 64 and k = 10, N − k = 54, so X[54] = (3 + 4j)* = 3 − 4j. The magnitude |X[k]| = 5 is the same at k and N − k, and the phases have opposite signs. For a real signal, therefore, the bins k = 0 to N/2 contain all the information in the spectrum.
choiceNotes: This flips the sign of the real part. The complex conjugate flips the sign of the imaginary part.
This is the same value as X[10]. The magnitude is the same, but the phase has the opposite sign.
Correct. X[N − k] is the complex conjugate of X[k].

dsp-016.question: The DFT of the 8-point real signal x[n] = {3, 1, 3, 1, 3, 1, 3, 1} is defined as X[k] = Σx[n]e^(−j2πkn/8). Which of the following is the value of X[4], the bin at the Nyquist frequency?
dsp-016.explanation: At k = N/2 = 4, e^(−jπn) = (−1)ⁿ, so X[4] = Σ(−1)ⁿx[n] = 3 − 1 + 3 − 1 + 3 − 1 + 3 − 1 = 8. The signal is a DC level of 2 plus a component (−1)ⁿ that alternates by ±1; the alternating component appears in the Nyquist bin and the DC level in X[0] = 16. For a real signal, X[0] and X[N/2] are always real.
choiceNotes: This is the amplitude of the alternating component (X[4]/N = 8/8). With this DFT definition, the value is N times larger.
This is the mean of the signal (the DC component, X[0]/N = 16/8).
Correct. Multiplying by (−1)ⁿ and summing gives 8.

dsp-017.question: Suppose an N-point DFT takes about N² operations when computed from its definition and about N log₂N operations with the FFT (fast Fourier transform). For N = 1024, which of the following is closest to the reduction in the number of operations achieved by the FFT?
dsp-017.explanation: N² = 1024² ≈ 1.05 million and N log₂N = 1024 × 10 = 10,240, so the ratio is N/log₂N = 1024 ÷ 10 = 102.4, about 1/100. The gap widens as N grows; for N = 65,536 the reduction is about 1/4096. The FFT reduces the work by repeatedly splitting a DFT into DFTs of half the size and sharing the common calculations.
choiceNotes: This is log₂N = 10. The ratio is N²/(N log₂N) = N/log₂N.
This is the ratio if the FFT took N operations (N²/N = 1024).

dsp-018.question: A 256-point signal is followed by 768 zeros (zero padding) and a 1024-point DFT is computed. Compared with computing the DFT of the 256 points as they are, which of the following is correct?
choices: The spectrum is interpolated at finer spacing, but the ability to tell apart two sine waves of close frequencies does not change
The bin spacing becomes 1/4, and the ability to tell apart two sine waves of close frequencies also improves fourfold
The added zeros join the two ends of the interval smoothly, so spectral leakage disappears and peak heights can be read accurately
dsp-018.explanation: Zero padding makes the bin spacing finer, fs/1024, and gives values interpolated between those of the 256-point spectrum. No new information is added, however, so the ability to tell two frequencies apart (the frequency resolution) is set by the 256 samples actually observed and stays at about fs/256. Truly improving it requires recording data over a longer time. Zero padding is used to make peak positions easier to read or to bring the number of points to a power of two for the FFT.
choiceNotes: Correct. The spectrum only looks smoother through interpolation; the ability to tell frequencies apart does not change.
The bin spacing becomes 1/4, but the ability to tell frequencies apart is set by the 256 samples observed and does not improve.
Leakage comes from how the observation interval is cut out, and appending zeros does not remove it.

dsp-019.question: Which of the following is the main cause of spectral leakage in a DFT?
choices: The sampling frequency is lower than twice the highest signal frequency, so high frequencies fold back onto low frequencies
When the number of DFT points is not a power of two, rounding errors in the FFT computation grow and spread to the surrounding bins
The observation interval does not contain a whole number of signal periods, so the waveform is treated as if its two ends joined discontinuously
dsp-019.explanation: The DFT treats the N observed points as one period of a repeating signal. If the interval holds exactly a whole number of periods of a sine wave, the peak fits in a single bin; otherwise the waveform is discontinuous where the ends of the interval meet, and that energy spreads into many surrounding bins. This is spectral leakage, and it can be reduced with a window function that brings both ends of the interval smoothly toward 0. Aliasing (folding) is a different phenomenon that occurs at sampling.
choiceNotes: This describes aliasing (folding), which is a different phenomenon from spectral leakage.
DFTs with a number of points that is not a power of two can be computed; only the FFT speed changes. Leakage is not caused by rounding errors.
Correct. The discontinuity at the ends of the interval spreads energy into the surrounding bins.

dsp-020.question: Which of the following correctly compares the rectangular window (no window applied) and the Hann (Hanning) window applied before a DFT?
choices: The Hann window makes the main lobe about half as wide as the rectangular window and also lowers the side lobes, so it is better in every respect
The Hann window has lower side lobes and less leakage into distant bins, but its main lobe is about twice as wide as that of the rectangular window
The Hann window narrows the main lobe, but in exchange its side lobes are higher than those of the rectangular window
dsp-020.explanation: The rectangular window has a narrow main lobe of ±1 bin (to the first nulls), but its highest side lobe is high, about −13 dB, so leakage spreads to distant bins. The Hann window brings both ends of the interval smoothly to 0, lowering the highest side lobe to about −31 dB, but its main lobe widens to ±2 bins, about twice as wide. The choice depends on the purpose: a window like Hann to see a weak signal near a strong one, and the rectangular window to tell apart signals of similar strength at close frequencies.
choiceNotes: The main lobe actually becomes wider. There is a trade-off: lowering the side lobes widens the main lobe.
Correct. The side lobes drop from about −13 dB to about −31 dB, and the main lobe widens from ±1 bin to ±2 bins.
It is the other way round: the Hann window has lower side lobes and a wider main lobe.

dsp-021.question: Assume the number of points N is large enough. In a DFT with a rectangular window, a sine wave lies exactly halfway between two adjacent bins. Which of the following is closest to the drop in the amplitude read at the nearest bin, compared with a sine wave exactly at a bin center?
dsp-021.explanation: With a rectangular window, a sine wave offset by δ bins from a bin center is read with sin(πδ)/(πδ) times its amplitude, and for δ = 0.5 this is sin(π/2)/(π/2) = 2/π ≈ 0.637. 20 log₁₀(0.637) ≈ −3.9 dB, so the amplitude can be read up to about 36% too low. This drop is called scalloping loss, and with a Hann window it is smaller, about 1.4 dB. For measurements that need accurate amplitudes, flat-top windows, whose main lobe has a flat top, are also used.
choiceNotes: This is the drop with a Hann window (about 1.42 dB). With a rectangular window the drop is larger.
Correct. 2/π ≈ 0.637, about −3.9 dB.
This is the value when the amplitude halves (about −6.0 dB). Halfway between bins the amplitude is 2/π ≈ 0.64 times.

dsp-022.question: The DFT of the 4-point signal x[n] = {1, −1, 2, 0} is defined as X[k] = Σx[n]e^(−j2πkn/4). Which of the following is Σ|X[k]|² (k = 0 to 3)?
dsp-022.explanation: By Parseval's theorem, Σ|X[k]|² = N·Σ|x[n]|² holds for a DFT with this definition. Since Σ|x[n]|² = 1 + 1 + 4 + 0 = 6, Σ|X[k]|² = 4 × 6 = 24. Computing X[k] = 2, −1 + j, 4, −1 − j directly gives |X[k]|² = 4, 2, 16, 2, which also sum to 24. The theorem states that energy is conserved (apart from the factor N) between the time side and the frequency side.
choiceNotes: This is Σ|x[n]|² = 6 divided by N = 4 (the average power per sample).
This is Σ|x[n]|² on the time side itself. With this DFT definition, the result is N = 4 times larger.
Correct. 4 × 6 = 24, which matches the X[k] computed directly.

dsp-023.question: When the frequency response of a discrete-time LTI system is obtained from its transfer function H(z), along which of the following is z moved?
choices: Along the unit circle of the z-plane (z = e^(jω), |z| = 1)
Along the positive real axis of the z-plane (z = r, where r is a real number greater than 0)
Along the imaginary axis of the z-plane (z = jω)
dsp-023.explanation: The frequency response is H(z) with z = e^(jω) substituted; as ω goes from −π to π, z travels once around the unit circle. z = 1 (ω = 0) corresponds to DC and z = −1 (ω = π) to the Nyquist frequency. For the continuous-time Laplace transform the frequency response is found on the imaginary axis s = jω, and in discrete time the unit circle plays that role.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is evaluated on the unit circle with z = e^(jω).
On the positive real axis, only the point z = 1 (DC), where it meets the unit circle, is part of the frequency response.
Evaluating on the imaginary axis applies to s of the continuous-time Laplace transform.

dsp-024.question: Which of the following is the transfer function H(z) = Y(z)/X(z) of the system described by the difference equation y[n] = x[n] + 0.5x[n − 1] + 0.25y[n − 1]?
dsp-024.explanation: A delay of one sample corresponds to multiplying by z⁻¹ in the z-transform, so transforming both sides gives Y(z) = X(z) + 0.5z⁻¹X(z) + 0.25z⁻¹Y(z). Collecting the Y(z) terms on the left gives (1 − 0.25z⁻¹)Y(z) = (1 + 0.5z⁻¹)X(z), so H(z) = (1 + 0.5z⁻¹)/(1 − 0.25z⁻¹). The numerator holds the coefficients on the input side and the denominator those of the output feedback; z = 0.25, which makes the denominator 0, is a pole, and z = −0.5, which makes the numerator 0, is a zero.
choiceNotes: This forgets to flip the sign of the coefficient when moving the feedback term to the left side.
This is the reciprocal of the correct H(z) (numerator and denominator swapped).
Correct. Moving the feedback term to the left side flips the sign of the denominator coefficient.

dsp-025.question: Which of the following correctly gives the poles and the stability of the causal system with transfer function H(z) = 1/(1 − 1.3z⁻¹ + 0.4z⁻²)?
choices: The poles are z = −0.5 and z = −0.8, and the system is stable
The poles are z = 0.5 and z = 0.8, and the system is stable
The poles are z = 1.25 and z = 2, and the system is unstable
dsp-025.explanation: Multiplying the numerator and denominator by z² gives H(z) = z²/(z² − 1.3z + 0.4), and the poles follow from z² − 1.3z + 0.4 = (z − 0.5)(z − 0.8) = 0 as z = 0.5 and 0.8. A causal system is stable when all its poles lie inside the unit circle (|z| < 1), so this system is stable. Solving the denominator as a polynomial in z⁻¹, 1 − 1.3p + 0.4p² = 0 (p = z⁻¹), gives p = 1.25, 2, but these are the reciprocals of the poles, not the poles themselves.
choiceNotes: The signs are wrong. The roots of z² − 1.3z + 0.4 = 0 are the positive values 0.5 and 0.8.
Correct. (z − 0.5)(z − 0.8) = z² − 1.3z + 0.4, and both poles lie inside the unit circle.
These solve the equation in z⁻¹ and are the reciprocals of the poles (1/0.8 = 1.25, 1/0.5 = 2).

dsp-026.question: An FIR filter with transfer function H(z) = 1 + z⁻² (y[n] = x[n] + x[n − 2]) runs at a sampling frequency of 8 kHz. Which of the following is the frequency of a sine-wave input for which the output is 0?
dsp-026.explanation: The solutions of 1 + z⁻² = 0, that is, the zeros, are z = ±j from z² = −1, which lie on the unit circle at ω = ±π/2. ω = π/2 corresponds to f = ω·fs/(2π) = fs/4 = 2 kHz; a 2 kHz sine wave has exactly the opposite sign two samples earlier, so the sum is 0. A zero on the unit circle creates a notch that completely removes that frequency. At 4 kHz (the Nyquist frequency), z⁻² = 1, so the gain is 2.
choiceNotes: At 1 kHz (ω = π/4), z⁻² = e^(−jπ/2) = −j and |1 − j| = √2 ≈ 1.41, so the output is not 0.
Correct. The zeros z = ±j lie at ω = π/2, that is, fs/4 = 2 kHz.
At the Nyquist frequency (z = −1), z⁻² = 1 and the gain is 1 + 1 = 2.

dsp-027.question: Which of the following gives the gain magnitudes at DC and at the Nyquist frequency of the filter y[n] = x[n] − x[n − 1] (the difference from the previous input)?
choices: 0 at DC and 2 at the Nyquist frequency
2 at DC and 0 at the Nyquist frequency
1 at DC and 1 at the Nyquist frequency
dsp-027.explanation: The transfer function is H(z) = 1 − z⁻¹; DC corresponds to z = 1 and the Nyquist frequency to z = −1. At DC, 1 − 1 = 0, so a constant value is completely removed, and at the Nyquist frequency the gain is 1 − (−1) = 2. This is a high-pass characteristic that blocks low frequencies and passes high ones, with a zero at z = 1. Changing it to y[n] = x[n] + x[n − 1] gives the opposite, a low-pass characteristic with a gain of 2 at DC and 0 at the Nyquist frequency.
choiceNotes: Correct. At z = 1, 1 − 1 = 0, and at z = −1, 1 + 1 = 2.
This is the characteristic of y[n] = x[n] + x[n − 1] (the sum of neighbors).
Taking the difference cancels DC to 0, and the gain at the Nyquist frequency is 2.

dsp-028.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of an FIR (finite impulse response) filter?
choices: It has feedback from the output to the input side, so a steep response can be obtained with few coefficients
Its impulse response continues forever, so it easily becomes unstable when its coefficients are quantized
It has no feedback, so it is always stable, and symmetric coefficients give it linear phase
dsp-028.explanation: An FIR filter only multiplies the present and past inputs by coefficients and adds them; it has no output feedback. Its impulse response ends after the number of coefficients (taps), and its poles lie only at z = 0, so it is stable whatever the coefficient values. With symmetric coefficients it has linear phase, delaying every frequency component by the same time and preserving the shape of the waveform. In exchange, a steep response needs more taps than an IIR filter.
choiceNotes: Feedback and a steep response with few coefficients are characteristics of IIR filters.
An infinitely long impulse response and possible instability from coefficient quantization belong to IIR filters.
Correct. Without feedback it is stable, and symmetric coefficients give linear phase.

dsp-029.question: Which of the following 5-tap FIR filters has linear phase?
dsp-029.explanation: If the coefficients of an FIR filter are symmetric about the center (h[n] = h[N − 1 − n]), the phase is a straight line proportional to frequency, and every frequency component is delayed by the same (N − 1)/2 samples. {1, 2, 3, 2, 1} is symmetric about the central 3, so it is a linear-phase filter with a constant delay of 2 samples. {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} and {5, 4, 3, 2, 1} are neither symmetric nor antisymmetric, so their delay changes with frequency.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is symmetric about the center, so the delay is a constant 2 samples.
The coefficients are not symmetric, so the delay changes with frequency.
This is just {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} reversed, and it is not symmetric either.

dsp-030.question: Which of the following is the group delay of a 101-tap linear-phase FIR filter (with symmetric coefficients)?
dsp-030.explanation: The group delay of an N-tap FIR filter with symmetric coefficients is (N − 1)/2 samples at every frequency. For N = 101 this is (101 − 1)/2 = 50 samples, the position of the center coefficient (the 51st coefficient, h[50]). At a sampling frequency of 48 kHz this is a delay of 50 ÷ 48000 ≈ 1.04 ms, and in real-time processing it must be kept in mind that more taps mean more delay.
choiceNotes: Correct. (101 − 1)/2 = 50 samples.
This is N/2 = 101/2. The delay is set by the position of the center coefficient, (N − 1)/2.
This is the number of taps itself (the full length of the impulse response). The delay is set by its center.

dsp-031.question: At a sampling frequency of 8 kHz, a moving-average filter y[n] = (x[n] + x[n − 1] + … + x[n − 7])/8 averages the latest 8 samples. Which of the following is the lowest frequency at which its output is 0?
dsp-031.explanation: The gain of an N-sample moving average is (1 + 1 + … + 1)/N = 1 at DC, and it is 0 at integer multiples of fs/N (other than DC). A sine wave at fs/N = 8000 ÷ 8 = 1 kHz completes exactly one cycle in 8 samples, so its average is 0. The moving average is a simple low-pass filter, but it has side lobes where the gain rises again between the nulls, so its cutoff is not very steep.
choiceNotes: This is fs/(2N) = 8000 ÷ 16. The first null is at fs/N.
Correct. At 1 kHz one cycle takes 8 samples, so the average is 0.
This is the Nyquist frequency. The output is 0 here too, but the lowest null is at 1 kHz.

dsp-032.question: Which of the following gives the gains at DC and at the Nyquist frequency of the first-order IIR low-pass filter given by the exponential smoothing y[n] = 0.2x[n] + 0.8y[n − 1]?
choices: 1 at DC and 0 at the Nyquist frequency
5 at DC and about 0.56 at the Nyquist frequency
1 at DC and about 0.11 at the Nyquist frequency
dsp-032.explanation: The transfer function is H(z) = 0.2/(1 − 0.8z⁻¹); at DC (z = 1) the gain is 0.2/(1 − 0.8) = 1, and at the Nyquist frequency (z = −1) it is 0.2/(1 + 0.8) = 1/9 ≈ 0.11 (about −19 dB). The new input is weighted by 0.2 and the previous output by 0.8; the weights sum to 1, so a constant input passes unchanged. Remembering only the previous output gives an average of past inputs with exponentially decreasing weights. The pole at z = 0.8 lies inside the unit circle, so the filter is stable, and the closer the feedback coefficient is to 1, the stronger the smoothing and the slower the response.
choiceNotes: The numerator of this filter is a constant and it has no zero on the unit circle, so there is no frequency where the gain is 0.
These are the gains of y[n] = x[n] + 0.8y[n − 1], with the input coefficient 0.2 replaced by 1 (1/0.2 = 5, 1/1.8 ≈ 0.56).

dsp-033.question: Which of the following correctly describes the bilinear transform used to design a digital filter from the transfer function H(s) of an analog filter?
choices: It maps the whole imaginary axis one-to-one onto the unit circle, so no aliasing occurs, but the frequency axis is warped, so important frequencies are corrected by prewarping
It samples the impulse response of the analog filter directly to obtain the coefficients, so high-frequency components fold back and change the response
It is the substitution z = 1 + sT, which approximates a derivative by a forward difference, so a stable analog filter always becomes a stable digital filter
dsp-033.explanation: The bilinear transform substitutes s = (2/T)(z − 1)/(z + 1); it maps the left half of the s-plane inside the unit circle, so a stable analog filter becomes a stable digital filter. The imaginary axis from 0 to ∞ maps one-to-one onto ω = 0 to π on the unit circle, so there is no aliasing, but the frequency axis is compressed according to Ω = (2/T)tan(ω/2). Important frequencies such as the cutoff frequency are therefore corrected with this relation in advance (prewarping) before the design. Sampling the impulse response is called the impulse-invariance method, and it does suffer from aliasing.
choiceNotes: Correct. There is no aliasing, but the frequency warping is corrected by prewarping.
This describes the impulse-invariance method. The bilinear transform causes no aliasing.
With z = 1 + sT (forward difference), a pole of a stable analog filter can map outside the unit circle, so stability is not guaranteed.

dsp-034.question: Which of the following is a correct precaution when implementing a high-order IIR filter in fixed point with coefficients of limited bit width?
choices: The poles of an IIR filter are not affected by coefficient quantization, so the coefficient bit width only needs to be chosen for passband gain accuracy
Like an FIR filter, it always stays stable after coefficient quantization, so even at high order it is best implemented as a single difference equation
Implementing the high-order denominator as a single expression lets coefficient errors move the poles and can make it unstable, so it is split into a cascade of second-order sections
dsp-034.explanation: The roots (poles) of a high-order polynomial are sensitive to tiny changes in its coefficients; especially in steep filters whose poles cluster near the unit circle, merely rounding the coefficients can push a pole outside the unit circle. Splitting the filter into second-order sections (biquads), each handling two poles, and connecting them in cascade keeps each section's coefficient errors from affecting the other poles, making it robust to quantization. An FIR filter stays stable after coefficient quantization, although its frequency response changes.
choiceNotes: The poles of an IIR filter are set by the denominator coefficients, and quantization moves them.
Only FIR filters, which have no feedback, always stay stable after quantization; IIR filters can become unstable.
Correct. A cascade of second-order sections makes the pole positions robust to coefficient errors.

dsp-035.question: A signal sampled at 48 kHz is reduced to 12 kHz by keeping one sample out of every four (decimation by 4). Which of the following frequency components should the low-pass filter placed before the downsampling remove?
dsp-035.explanation: After downsampling, the sampling frequency is 48 ÷ 4 = 12 kHz and its Nyquist frequency is 6 kHz. If components above 6 kHz remain when the samples are dropped, they fold back under 12 kHz sampling and overlap the band below 6 kHz (for example, a 9 kHz component appears at 12 − 9 = 3 kHz). A digital low-pass filter therefore attenuates everything above 6 kHz sufficiently before the downsampling.
choiceNotes: Correct. Everything above the new Nyquist frequency of 6 kHz is removed.
This is the new sampling frequency itself. The folding boundary is half of it, 6 kHz.
This is the Nyquist frequency of the original 48 kHz. The original signal has no components above 24 kHz anyway, so this alone does not prevent aliasing.

dsp-036.question: To raise the sampling frequency by a factor of L, L − 1 zeros are inserted between successive samples (zero insertion). Which of the following correctly describes the processing needed next?
choices: Inserting zeros creates low-frequency components not present in the original signal, so a high-pass filter is applied to remove those low-frequency components
Images (copies of the spectrum) appear around integer multiples of the original sampling frequency, so a low-pass filter removes them and the gain is multiplied by L
Inserting zeros creates no new components in the spectrum, so no filter is needed and the result can be used directly as a signal at the new sampling frequency
dsp-036.explanation: After zero insertion, copies (images) of the original spectrum appear on the new frequency axis around integer multiples of the original sampling frequency fs. For example, zero-inserting a 1 kHz sine wave sampled at fs = 8 kHz with L = 2 produces a component at 8 − 1 = 7 kHz as well as at 1 kHz. Removing them with a low-pass filter that cuts at the original Nyquist frequency fs/2 (an anti-imaging or interpolation filter) fills the zeros with smooth interpolated values. The inserted zeros reduce the amplitude to 1/L, so the filter gain is set to L to restore the original amplitude.
choiceNotes: What must be removed are the images that appear at high frequencies, and the filter used is a low-pass filter.
Correct. A low-pass filter removes the images, and a gain of L restores the amplitude.
The images remain and the waveform stays interspersed with zeros, so a filter is needed.

dsp-037.question: To convert the sampling frequency from 44.1 kHz to 48 kHz, upsampling by L and downsampling by 1/M are combined. Which of the following is the smallest pair of integers (L, M)?
dsp-037.explanation: The required ratio is 48/44.1 = 48000/44100 = 480/441, which reduces by the greatest common divisor 3 to 160/147 (160 = 2⁵ × 5 and 147 = 3 × 7², so it cannot be reduced further). Upsampling by 160 to 7.056 MHz, low-pass filtering and then downsampling by 1/147 gives 48 kHz. In practice, polyphase structures and the like compute only the outputs that are needed, avoiding computing everything at 7.056 MHz.
choiceNotes: L and M are swapped, giving 44.1 kHz × 147/160 ≈ 40.5 kHz.
The ratio is right, but it can be reduced by 3, so it is not the smallest pair.
Correct. 44.1 kHz × 160/147 = 48 kHz.

dsp-038.question: A 256-tap FIR filter runs in real time at a sampling frequency of 44.1 kHz. Which of the following is the number of multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations needed per second?
dsp-038.explanation: An FIR filter performs as many multiply-accumulates per output sample as it has taps, here 256. There are 44,100 outputs per second, so 256 × 44,100 = 11,289,600, about 11.3 million MACs are needed. Even a processor that performs one MAC per cycle needs a clock of at least about 11.3 MHz, and in practice work such as reading and writing data is added.
choiceNotes: This is the number of outputs per second (the sampling frequency) itself. Each output needs 256 MACs.
Correct. 256 × 44,100 ≈ 11.3 million.
This counts multiplications and additions separately (2 × 256 × 44,100). Counting a MAC as one operation gives half of it.

dsp-039.question: An FIR filter output is computed for every sample at a sampling frequency of 48 kHz on a processor clocked at 200 MHz that performs one multiply-accumulate per cycle. Ignoring the time for other processing, which of the following is closest to the maximum number of taps that can be processed in real time?
dsp-039.explanation: The time available per sample is 1/48000 ≈ 20.8 µs, which is 200 MHz ÷ 48 kHz ≈ 4167 clock cycles. At one MAC per cycle, about 4,170 taps can be computed. If this time is exceeded, the output is not ready before the next sample arrives and real-time processing breaks down, so in practice designs leave a margin for interrupts, data transfers and the like.
choiceNotes: This assumes one cycle each for the multiplication and the addition (4167 ÷ 2). This processor performs a MAC in one cycle.
Correct. 200 MHz ÷ 48 kHz ≈ 4167 cycles.
This divides by the Nyquist frequency of 24 kHz instead of the sampling frequency (200 MHz ÷ 24 kHz).

dsp-040.question: In an FIR filter computation, products of 16-bit fixed-point data and coefficients are represented in 32 bits, and 256 of these products are added up. Which of the following is the minimum accumulator width that guarantees no overflow during the computation?
dsp-040.explanation: Adding two 32-bit products can increase the magnitude by up to 1 bit, and adding 256 = 2⁸ of them by up to 8 bits. An accumulator of 32 + log₂256 = 32 + 8 = 40 bits therefore cannot overflow even in the worst case. Some typical 16-bit fixed-point DSPs have 40-bit accumulators, with 8 guard bits added to the 32-bit product. When the result is finally brought back to 16 bits, rounding and saturating arithmetic keep it within range.
choiceNotes: With the same 32 bits as the product, adding just two products can overflow.
A 1-bit margin guarantees only the sum of two products.
Correct. 256 = 2⁸, so 8 guard bits are added for 40 bits.
